title: Inboard advance of arc magmatism regulates mountain building in the Andes

paper_content.abstract: Debate continues over the mechanisms that govern the tempo and style of arc magmatism and retroarc deformation along ocean-continent plate boundaries. Here we integrate detrital and bedrock geo/thermochronological and geochemical records of Cenozoic arc magmatism with results on the spatiotemporal evolution of retroarc shortening and flexural subsidence to explore the interactions and feedbacks among subduction, magmatism, and crustal deformation in the southern Central Andes. A synthesis of igneous compositions, magmatic activity, thrust belt shortening, and sediment accumulation reveals recurring phases of increased arc magmatism, retroarc underthrusting, and foreland basin development over short (<10 Myr) timescales. Episodic advance of deformation was focused within discrete Andean tectonic provinces (of contrasting pre-Andean inheritance) that were sequentially activated toward the foreland along newly formed middle/upper-crustal décollements. Inboard migration of arc magmatism consistently preceded deformation advance, suggesting that fluid-assisted weakening above the subducting slab facilitated enhanced shortening and orogenic growth toward the cratonic interior.
paper_content.introduction:
Interactions between arc magmatism and retroarc deformation shape topography, climate, and basin evolution in Andean-type orogenic systems along ocean-continent convergent margins. These relationships may represent responses to external drivers and/or internally coordinated processes that strongly influence crustal shortening, igneous activity, and basin subsidence. The underlying mechanisms responsible for time-space variations in tectonic and magmatic processes remain poorly understood. Most models linking the rates and magnitudes of arc magmatism and retroarc deformation have centered on cyclical behavior in orogens characterized by large-scale (>200–300 km) horizontal shortening, extreme crustal thickening (>60–70 km Moho depth), and episodic removal of thickened lower crust/lithosphere through foundering or delamination1,2,3,4. Such cycles occur over long timescales (>20–50 Myr) and preferentially affect only the largest and thickest orogenic systems. However, potential internal cycles of shorter duration (<10 Myr) may also operate during mountain building, particularly in regions of lower-magnitude (<50–150 km) shortening. Here we hypothesize that short-term orogenic phases linked to shifts in thermal and rheological conditions help regulate dynamic interactions among subduction, arc magmatism, and retroarc deformation.

Evaluating Andean-type orogenesis requires consideration of diverse mechanisms that affect spatial-temporal patterns in arc magmatism and retroarc shortening. Arc migration toward the continental interior has been associated with heightened magmatic activity along subduction margins5. Such landward migration expands slab dewatering within the mantle wedge, enhancing fluid flux and hydration of the overriding foreland lithosphere6, which may further induce crustal weakening and strain localization7.

A range of internal and external mechanisms within the upper and lower plates may account for inboard advance of arc magmatism8. Internally, within the overriding plate, arc advance may be a product of retroarc shortening9 and/or forearc subduction erosion 10,11. In addition, arc advance may be driven by external forces that affect the subducting plate, including accelerated plate convergence12 or low-angle (flat slab) subduction13,14,15,16. Although slab shallowing is commonly attributed to subduction of buoyant (i.e., younger or thicker) oceanic lithosphere, several studies indicate a poor correlation among oceanic slab age, crustal thickness, seafloor asperities, and slab dip17,18. Alternatively, slab shallowing may be driven by the position of thick continental lithospheric roots that promote hydrodynamic suction (or negative pressure) associated with corner flow in the mantle wedge between the subducting and overriding plates 19,20. Because the aforementioned interactions vary over a range of spatial and temporal scales, it is important to identify the processes responsible for arc migration and assess their impact on short-term (<10 Myr) changes in magmatism and retroarc orogenesis within Cordilleran systems.

In this study, we compare the spatial, temporal, and compositional variations of arc magmatism in the southern Central Andes with geo/thermochronological, geochemical, and stratigraphic datasets to better understand the geodynamic links among subduction, magmatism, and Andean orogenesis. The modern Pampean segment (27–33° S) of the Nazca-South American plate boundary (Fig. 1) is characterized by flat slab subduction, a ~500 km long gap in active volcanism, and foreland basement uplifts of the Sierras Pampeanas located >700 km inboard of the trench (Fig. 1A)15, 21, 22, 23, 24. Our analysis focuses on the past 30 Myr of mountain building in western Argentina, a region characterized by persistently arid climatic conditions25,26, which enables the isolation of tectonic signals associated with orogenic wedge behavior. Synthesizing records of Andean arc magmatism and retroarc deformation provides the opportunity to explore the feedbacks between subducting and overriding plates to identify potentially cyclical mechanisms that regulate mountain building along convergent plate boundaries.
paper_content.results:
Magmatic Arc Activity and Composition

To assess time-space patterns of arc magmatism and retroarc crustal shortening, we compile crystallization ages of Cenozoic igneous rocks along an arc-normal east-west profile (Fig. 2A). These regional patterns in arc magmatism (Fig. 2A) are compared with arc tempo and magmatic compositional data registered in whole-rock and zircon minerals (Fig. 3B and 3C). Geochronological results paired with εHf and εNd isotopic compositions provide valuable temporal recorders of continental arc evolution that are sensitive to upper-crustal composition and crystallization conditions. Positive εHf and εNd values reflect juvenile crustal material originating from melts of depleted (juvenile) mantle origin, whereas negative isotopic values signify enriched melts derived from older, recycled (evolved) crustal material27, 28, 29.

The geochemical match between detrital zircon εHf values and those of spatially resolved igneous bedrock (Fig. 3A) strengthens confidence in their provenance and demonstrates their value as a complementary tool for tracking magmatic evolution through time. Detrital zircon age distributions for continental magmatic arcs and their associated basins are robust temporal indicators of arc activity, suitable for tracking rates of zircon-bearing arc-magma production and identifying punctuated high-volume magmatic events in the form of flare-ups or high-flux events (HFEs)30,31,32.

Oligocene arc magmatism (33–25 Ma) was focused over a narrow (~100 km wide) zone within the Main Cordillera (Fig. 2A). Compositionally, these magmas exhibit positive εHf and εNd values, indicative of depleted mantle wedge sources (Fig. 3B). By 25 Ma, the arc advanced eastward, forming a broader (~200 km wide) zone that spanned the Main and Frontal Cordilleras (Fig. 2A). During the late Oligocene to early Miocene (25–19 Ma) zircon εHf trends delineate an isotopic pull-down toward enriched magma sources contemporaneous with increased arc activity recorded by greater proportions of detrital zircon ages (Fig. 3B and 3C). From 19 to 13 Ma, early to middle Miocene magmatism expanded eastward into the Precordillera (Fig. 2A). At this time, zircon εHf and whole-rock εNd results exhibited further isotopic pull-down from positive (depleted) to negative (enriched) values coeval with increased arc activity (Fig. 3B and 3C). A broad swath of magmatism was activated at 13–6 Ma, indicating rapid eastward advance (>400 km) of magmatism toward the craton. Arc geochemical data again recorded a shift to lower (enriched) values synchronous with heightened arc magmatism (Fig. 3B and 3C). At ~5 Ma, a notable cessation of arc magmatism occurred within the Main and Frontal Cordilleras (71–69° W), the former locus of Neogene magmatism.

Coupled geochemical and age data from igneous and detrital samples exhibit a progressive decrease in zircon εHf and whole-rock εNd values over the past 30 Myr (Fig. 3B), reflecting the cumulative effects of crustal thickening driven by sustained shortening during Andean orogenesis. When considered alongside bedrock sample locations (Fig. 2A), a spatial relationship emerges: relatively asthenospheric (juvenile) compositions are preferentially situated near the trench, while more lithospheric (evolved) contributions are concentrated toward the craton (Fig. 3B). This spatial gradient manifests as temporal variability, as the magmatic arc migrated eastward into older continental lithosphere with distinct isotopic signatures. Superimposed on this long-term (30 Myr) trend are higher-frequency phases (5–8 Myr) marked by transient shifts in εHf and εNd values. These phases represent background arc magmatism sourced from juvenile mantle, periodically perturbed during isotopic pull-downs that recorded increased crustal contamination and partial melting during phases of shortening and underthrusting (Fig. 3B). At the onset of each pull down, a 1–2 Myr temporal overlap of depleted and enriched values suggests magma mixing processes during transitions in source contributions33. Together, these patterns underscore the dual influence of arc migration into older lithosphere and progressive crustal thickening in shaping the isotopic evolution of Andean magmatism.

Retroarc Shortening and Flexural Response

Structural kinematic records, low-temperature thermochronologic data, and foreland subsidence histories collectively document the timing and style of retroarc shortening, exhumation, and crustal loading. First, thermochronometric results constrain bedrock cooling in response to upper crustal erosion (Fig. 2A). Apatite fission track (AFT) and (U-Th)/He (AHe) thermochronometric dates are based on temperature-dependent diffusive loss of radiogenic daughter products or fission damage trails and record mineral cooling below ~40–120°C. These systems are sensitive to exhumation history of rocks within approximately 6 km of the surface34. Second, eastward migration of the retroarc foreland basin during construction of the southern Central Andes provides an independent means of tracking deformation advance35,36. Third, sediment accumulation histories along an arc-normal transect of basin sections are leveraged to highlight spatial-temporal changes in the flexural response to retroarc shortening during sequential activation of discrete contractional systems toward the foreland (Fig. 3D).

The upper crustal tectonic regime varied throughout Cenozoic subduction. During the middle Eocene to early Oligocene, intra-arc transtensional faulting governed basin formation37, 38, 39. Subsequent late Oligocene–early Miocene shortening accompanied increased convergence along the subduction margin during breakup of the oceanic Farallon plate into the Nazca and Cocos plates (Fig. 2B)40,41. This tectonic shift coincided with the main phase of Andean shortening, which was accommodated in the Main (Principal) Cordillera by thin-skinned shortening and inversion of Triassic to Paleogene extensional and retroarc basin fill39,42.

Rapid foreland subsidence in western basin sites (i.e., Calingasta, Talacasto, and Manantiales) initiated by 24–22 Ma in response to shortening in the Main Cordillera43,26. Thereafter, deformation advanced eastward to deeper structural levels of the Frontal Cordillera, where reverse faults exhumed mechanical basement composed of a >3 km thick panel of Permian-Triassic rhyolitic and granitic rocks (Choiyoi Group) associated with the pre-Andean Cuyo rift system44,45. Accelerated sediment accumulation at 19–13 Ma recorded foredeep development during shortening, uplift, and thrust loading in the Frontal Cordillera46,43. Thermochronology and sediment provenance data reveal an eastward progression of exhumation within the orogenic wedge from the Andean hinterland (Main Cordillera and Frontal Cordillera) to the thin-skinned Precordillera thrust belt by 16 Ma47,48. Precordillera shortening was characterized by imbricate faults that deformed a Paleozoic stratigraphic wedge above a regional décollement along the basement-cover interface49,50. From 13 to 7 Ma, the foredeep migrated eastward while 65–100 km of E-W shortening was accommodated in the Precordillera36, 47, 51, 52. Coeval cooling in the hinterland suggests passive exhumation as the trailing thrust sheet was translated over a mid-crustal ramp that links eastward into the Precordillera décollement53, 54.

By 6 Ma, shortening-induced exhumation advanced eastward into the Sierras Pampeanas, where intraforeland basement-cored uplifts developed above crustal-scale reverse faults15, 55, 56. Diminished sediment accumulation after ~7 Ma in the eastern foreland reflects a transition to broken foreland conditions, as Sierras Pampeanas basement uplifts partitioned the once-continuous foreland basin into disconnected depocenters57, 58.
paper_content.methods: The spatial distribution of magmatism is constrained by an extensive compilation (n=741; Supplemental Data 1) of Eocene to Pleistocene bedrock radiometric ages at 27°–32.5° S (Fig. 2A)82. Data curation involved calculating a mean age for igneous samples and omittance of duplicate and detrital ages. The spatial and temporal distributions of igneous ages are plotted on Supplemental Figure 1. Whole-rock εHf data derive from an igneous bedrock compilation (n=28)85 across Argentina, whereas the zircon εHf values are from both igneous bedrock (n=128)86 and detrital zircon samples (n=44)24 spanning the Chile-Argentina hinterland and retroarc regions to the east (Fig. 3B; Supplementary Data 2 and Supplementary Data 3). All geochemical data were plotted using Hafnium Plotter software87. The detrital zircon U-Pb age distribution representing Andean arc activity comes from a Phanerozoic compilation (Fig. 3C)24. Compilated mean AHe (n=103) and central AFT (n=53) thermochronology dates are an aggregate of both crystalline and sedimentary samples across the southern Central Andes 27–32.5° S (Fig. 2A; Supplementary Data 4; Supplementary Data 5). Filtering of apatite (U-Th-Sm)/He and fission track dates adheres to rejection criteria that excludes anonymously low He concentrations, un-reset dates, high date dispersion, date outlier, and overlap with igneous age or proximal hydrothermal activity. The spatial distributions of thermochronometric ages are plotted in Supplemental Figure 2, while single grain ages of the mean AHe samples (Fig. 2A) are plotted in Supplemental Figure A3. Structural constraints on faulting in the arc and retroarc regions are supported by synorogenic stratigraphic, structural, cross-cutting relationships, thermochronology data, and thermokinematic modeling (Fig. 2A; Supplementary Data 6). Sediment accumulation rates are calculated from seven basin locations (Fig. 1) with previously measured stratigraphic sections and associated age constraints (Fig. 3D; Supplementary Data 7).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This contribution by Capaldi and coauthors integrates geo/thermochronological, geochemical and stratigraphic records of Cenozoic arc magmatism to shed light on the interplay between subduction dynamics, arc magmatism, back-arc crustal shortening and flexural subsidence in Andean-type subduction orogens. To achieve this, a compilation of igneous rock crystallization ages, combined with zircon U-Pb geochronology and εHf isotopic compositions, provides valuable insights into the mechanisms governing these complex geological processes.
The manuscript presents a compelling case for the role of short-term (5-8 Myr) tectonic-magma cycles in controlling deformation and foreland basin subsidence. This represents a significant advancement over previous models that have primarily focused on longer (10-20 Myr) episodes of magmatism, deformation and crustal thickening. The discussion on how these shorter cycles particularly affect regions with lower magnitudes of shortening is insightful and adds an important dimension to our understanding of Andean orogenesis.
Overall, this paper is well-framed, clear, concisely written and technically sound. However, I have a few suggestions that might enhance its clarity and impact:
• The timing of εHf isotopic variations could be more precisely constrained. For instance, in Figure 3, while the trend between 28 Ma and 22 Ma is well-explained, the period between 25-22 Ma shows both positive and negative εHf values, suggesting contributions from both depleted-mantle and enriched-crustal melts. A discussion of the possible causes in the text for this mixed signal would be beneficial.
• The second pull-down phase (19-13 Ma) is linked to the expansion of arc magmatism into the Precordillera. However, the isotopic pull-down appears to begin after 16-17 Ma. A clarification of this apparent discrepancy would be helpful.
• The subsidence of the Talacasto Basin, located far from the thrust front in the Main Cordillera, is intriguing. The absence of similar subsidence evidence in the Calingasta and Manantiales Basins at the eastern foot of the Frontal Cordillera also warrants further discussion.
• Figure 4: This is an excellent and self-explanatory figure. I suggest incorporating a time-referencing framework from the Southern Central Andes example to provide additional and specific context for different phases.
Additional points for consideration on this Figure:
• Why is there no lithospheric mantle beneath the arc axis in Step 1? I suggest changing the figure or explaining why not?
• In Step 2, could you elaborate on how fluids migrate to the retroarc region?
• In Step 3, does the model require a normal or thin crust? Could you expand on how flexural subsidence in the foreland relates to shortening?
Minor issues:
• Abstract: Clarify why magmatism migrates in your model and whether slab flattening is a necessary condition or not.
• Line 51: Further explain why landward arc magmatism migration enhances fluid flux.
• Lines 67-69: The phrase "spatial and temporal variations" could be more specific.
• Line 104: The study focuses on the relationship between arc magmatism and retroarc crustal shortening, rather than broad crustal deformation. Please correct.
• Lines 115-117: Address the proposed crustal extension during the late Oligocene-Early Miocene (25-20 Ma).
• Lines 119-129: Discuss the isotopic pull-up periods (21-18 Ma, 13-11 Ma, 7-6 Ma), which are visible in Figure 3 but not explained in the text.
• Lines 157-158: Clarify the timing of major subsidence and its correlation with the Main Cordillera shortening.
• Line 160: Define "high-angle reverse faults" more clearly.
• Lines 204-206: Could you specify which retroarc regions are weakened by slab-derived fluids?
• Line 210: The term "High-Flux Events (HFEs)" should be introduced earlier with an explanation.
• Figure 1: Add basin names to the caption.
Overall, this is a valuable contribution to the field. However, addressing the points above would further strengthen the manuscript and clarify key interpretations. I would strongly encourage publication, following these refinements.
Best regards,
Laura Giambiagi
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Dear Editor,
In this letter I send you my comments on the paper entitled “Inboard advance of arc magmatism regulates mountain building in the Andes” coauthored by Capaldi, T., Horton, B., Mackaman-Lofland, C., Fuentes, F. and Ortiz, G.
This work explores the interactions and feedbacks among subduction, magmatism, and crustal deformation in a continental margin setting taking as a case study the southern Central Andes, mostly between ~29°-33°S. It is based on an extensive compilation of data that includes igneous ages, apatite (U-Th-Sm)/He and fission track thermochronology, and zircon Hf isotopic composition, in addition to calculations of sediment accumulation rates and deformation front reconstructions also based on the information reported by previous studies. The main text of the manuscript is well organized, the 4 figures included are appropriate to illustrate the issues discussed, and there is an extensive supplementary material which provides the data on which the work is based. I do consider that the figures and the supplementary material could be improved (see below).
As a main result, the work proposes a cyclic model that links short-term orogenic phases with shifts in thermal and rheological processes with the following sequential events: (1) arc magmatism weakens the crust, (2) the latter can then be deformed mostly by retroarc shortening with westward underthrusting, (3) crustal thickening prompts slab shallowing and a consequent eastward arc migration, (4) the newly allocated arc starts the cycle again. The model is very appealing as it offers a linked explanation of major processes observed throughout Andean orogenic construction: the eastward migration of arc magmatism and of deformation. In addition, as stated in the manuscript itself, the model focuses on internal orogenic cycles much shorter (<10 Myr) and of less magnitude (<50-150 km horizontal shortening) than those already covered in previous works (>20-50 Ma and >200-300 km horizontal shortening; e.g. Haschke et al., 2002; DeCelles et al., 2009; DeCelles and Graham, 2015; Balgord et al., 2021).
The model proposed in this work is supported by showing how the eastward migration of the deformation front coincides with aspects as increased accumulation rates in the retroarc foreland basins, temporal trends in magmatic activity, and compositional changes in the arc magmas based on the Hf isotopic composition. It is regarding this last issue that I consider the model has a major flaw, as the data is being carelessly interpreted. It must be noted that the Hf data presented in this work is from two sources: (1) the work of Jones et al. (2015), analyses performed in zircons from Cenozoic igneous rocks, and (2) the work of Capaldi et al. (2021), analyses performed in detrital zircons.
As described in Jones et al. (2015), Cenozoic igneous rocks in this region display a clear pattern of more enriched signatures (more “crustal like”) towards the east, as shown by mostly coeval units emplaced in the Frontal Cordillera and the Precordillera. This was ascribed by the authors to the presence of an old basement in the eastern regions (Grenvillian Basement – Cuyania Terrane?) responsible to imprint the enriched signature to the magmas that have transversed it in the eastern region (Precordillera). This had been also recognized earlier by Kay and Abbruzzi (1996) on this same region and by Muñoz et al. (2013) on central Chile (~34°S). A quick look at the data presented in the manuscript that considers the lithologies and the sample location, will reveal that: (1) rocks emplaced in the Frontal Cordillera describe, by themselves, a pattern towards enriched ƐHf signatures from ~28 to 6 Ma, and these data is the one mostly controlling the pattern in blue presented in the ƐHf vs Age diagram in the manuscript, (2) rocks emplaced in the Precordillera also define a pattern towards more enriched ƐHf signatures in time but in a comparatively lower ƐHf trend (more enriched than that of the Frontal Cordillera; note there are also minor juvenile inputs), and these are the samples that mostly control the pattern in red presented in the ƐHf vs Age diagram in the manuscript, (3) the detrital zircon data is a “disperse cloud” that encompasses both patterns previously described. The detrital data, for which there is no precise knowledge of the zircon source (location in the Andean orogen), is not reliable for the analysis/interpretations presented by the authors, as the “location” of the arc at any stage cannot be stablished. The ƐHf vs Age diagram presented by the authors is showing: (1) the basement control over the composition of Cenozoic Andean arc magmas, with those emplaced in the Frontal Cordillera being less enriched than those emplaced further east in the Precordillera (respectively the patterns in blue and in red in the diagram), and (2) the progressive enrichment that Cenozoic Andean magmas have suffered throughout the progressive crustal thickening that accompanies the construction of the modern orogen (the general patterns towards higher ƐHf signatures in time, in both areas).
Even though the models just described from Kay et al. (2005), Muñoz et al. (2013) and Jones et al. (2015) were not valid, the ƐHf vs Age interpretation of the manuscript is still not sustained. For example, the latest “arc event” recorded in ƐHf basis (~5-8 Ma; ƐHf: ~0 to -3) is indeed more juvenile than the immediately preceding event (~8-11 Ma; ƐHf: ~ -3 to -5), yet the samples defining the former are in a western location (Frontal Cordillera) respect the those defining the latter (Precordillera). This is the opposite to that indicated by the model of the manuscript, where the juvenile newly stablished arc is eastwards, and the same happens when looking in detail the older age data.
Regarding figures: (1) Fig. 1b is too overloaded with geological units and could be simplified, (2) in Fig. 2B the text within the diagrams is too small, (3) the third panel to the right in Fig 2 seems to be missing the “C”, (3) in Fig. 4 there should be an indication of what means/signals the black segmented line oval. I note also some problems with the supplementary material. First, the citation to the tables in the manuscript, in the Methods section, is wrong with respect to the labeling in the excel sheet containing the data. In the excel sheet itself: (1) “Table 1-Ign Ages” has text in Spanish and in English, (2) “Table 4 Zircon Hf” has no information on sample location. In this last case, such information can be readily found for the samples of Jones et al. (2015) in that work, but this is not the case for several samples from Capaldi et al. (2021; not found in that paper nor in the www.geochron.org; samples TAL06, TAL06m, TAL16, TAL14, TAL09, RAG01, RSJc01, ST02). This issue hampers a proper evaluation of the data analyzed in the manuscript and consequently of the conclusions drawn from it.
Best regards.

Response to reviewer comments/suggestions
This document provides a detailed, point-by-point response to comments from reviewers associated with the original submission of this manuscript to Nature Communications (NCOMMS-24-86680).
Our responses below are shown in BOLD and line numbers refer to the revised manuscript.
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This contribution by Capaldi and coauthors integrates geo/thermochronological, geochemical and stratigraphic records of Cenozoic arc magmatism to shed light on the interplay between subduction dynamics, arc magmatism, back-arc crustal shortening and flexural subsidence in Andean-type subduction orogens. To achieve this, a compilation of igneous rock crystallization ages, combined with zircon U-Pb geochronology and εHf isotopic compositions, provides valuable insights into the mechanisms governing these complex geological processes.
The manuscript presents a compelling case for the role of short-term (5-8 Myr) tectonic-magma cycles in controlling deformation and foreland basin subsidence. This represents a significant advancement over previous models that have primarily focused on longer (10-20 Myr) episodes of magmatism, deformation and crustal thickening. The discussion on how these shorter cycles particularly affect regions with lower magnitudes of shortening is insightful and adds an important dimension to our understanding of Andean orogenesis.
Overall, this paper is well-framed, clear, concisely written and technically sound. However, I have a few suggestions that might enhance its clarity and impact:
We thank the reviewer for their insights and critical evaluation of our work.
The timing of εHf isotopic variations could be more precisely constrained. For instance, in Figure 3, while the trend between 28 Ma and 22 Ma is well-explained, the period between 25-22 Ma shows both positive and negative εHf values, suggesting contributions from both depleted-mantle and enriched-crustal melts. A discussion of the possible causes in the text for this mixed signal would be beneficial.
You make a good point. We have elaborated on the potential for magma mixing during progressive change in magmatic sources during this 1 to 2 Myr overlap in zircon εHf values. See lines 135-138.
The second pull-down phase (19-13 Ma) is linked to the expansion of arc magmatism into the Precordillera. However, the isotopic pull-down appears to begin after 16-17 Ma. A clarification of this apparent discrepancy would be helpful.
Yes there are apparent lag times between arc advance, retroarc shortening, and resulting change in arc magmatism. Our multi-phase model attempts to address the sequence of events where arc migration is temporally followed by shortening which induces a high-flux event in the magmatic arc. Although we don’t directly link the Central Andes data to the model the 16 Ma isotopic pull down follows arc expansion around 19 Ma, we address the temporal overlap in both depleted and enriched values reflecting magma mixing during changes in magmatic sources. Line 130-140.
The subsidence of the Talacasto Basin, located far from the thrust front in the Main Cordillera, is intriguing. The absence of similar subsidence evidence in the Calingasta and Manantiales Basins at the eastern foot of the Frontal Cordillera also warrants further discussion.
The seemingly early initiation and relatively higher subsidence rates of the Talacasto Basin are the result of the Oligocene-Miocene erg system that developed in the Precordilleran region (Starck et al., 2023). When looking along strike the Talacasto basin history is comparable to the Las Juntas (La Troya) system to the North (Reynolds et al., 1990; Cicioli et al., 2014; Mackaman-Lofland et al., 2020). But you bring up a good point about Manantiales and Calingasta, why don’t we see a similar subsidence pattern? One option could be our age constraints of the lower intervals are relatively sparse. In Mananitales the basal Rio de Los Patos Formation has good age constraints in the lower part dating back to the Eocene but lack constraints in the upper unit (Suriano et al., 2023). The same can be said about the Calingasta location where there several > 10 Myr gaps in age data in the lower section, which provides low resolution of foreland basin initiation there (Capaldi et al., 2020). In this context, we may be “missing” the data that would indicate basin initiation in line with what is known from Talacasto. Another option, albeit more speculative, may involve as-yet-underappreciated complex paleotopography underlying the basin system. To the east, in the Bermejo Basin, we observed along strike variation in the timing of basin initiation as the result of paleotopographic highs (Plonka et al., 2023). Perhaps Talacasto preserves an appreciable amount of low paleotopography that was infilled by eolian facies, while the western Calingasta and Manantiales Basins represented a net-transport system until flexurally-induced subsidence initiated in the early Miocene. All of this is intended to reinforce the point that Talacasto fits into the paradigm of our understanding of the foreland basin system here, but we have considered these nuances and agree with the reviewer regarding their importance. However, given the target audience and primary focus for this manuscript, we will hold off on such detailed speculation until the sequel manuscript.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this letter I send you my comments on the paper entitled “Inboard advance of arc magmatism regulates mountain building in the Andes” coauthored by Capaldi, T., Horton, B., Mackaman-Lofland, C., Fuentes, F. and Ortiz, G.
This work explores the interactions and feedbacks among subduction, magmatism, and crustal deformation in a continental margin setting taking as a case study the southern Central Andes, mostly between ~29°-33°S. It is based on an extensive compilation of data that includes igneous ages, apatite (U-Th-Sm)/He and fission track thermochronology, and zircon Hf isotopic composition, in addition to calculations of sediment accumulation rates and deformation front reconstructions also based on the information reported by previous studies. The main text of the manuscript is well organized, the 4 figures included are appropriate to illustrate the issues discussed, and there is an extensive supplementary material which provides the data on which the work is based. I do consider that the figures and the supplementary material could be improved (see below).
As a main result, the work proposes a cyclic model that links short-term orogenic phases with shifts in thermal and rheological processes with the following sequential events: (1) arc magmatism weakens the crust, (2) the latter can then be deformed mostly by retroarc shortening with westward underthrusting, (3) crustal thickening prompts slab shallowing and a consequent eastward arc migration, (4) the newly allocated arc starts the cycle again. The model is very appealing as it offers a linked explanation of major processes observed throughout Andean orogenic construction: the eastward migration of arc magmatism and of deformation. In addition, as stated in the manuscript itself, the model focuses on internal orogenic cycles much shorter (<10 Myr) and of less magnitude (<50-150 km horizontal shortening) than those already covered in previous works (>20-50 Ma and >200-300 km horizontal shortening; e.g. Haschke et al., 2002; DeCelles et al., 2009; DeCelles and Graham, 2015; Balgord et al., 2021).
The model proposed in this work is supported by showing how the eastward migration of the deformation front coincides with aspects as increased accumulation rates in the retroarc foreland basins, temporal trends in magmatic activity, and compositional changes in the arc magmas based on the Hf isotopic composition. It is regarding this last issue that I consider the model has a major flaw, as the data is being carelessly interpreted. It must be noted that the Hf data presented in this work is from two sources: (1) the work of Jones et al. (2015), analyses performed in zircons from Cenozoic igneous rocks, and (2) the work of Capaldi et al. (2021), analyses performed in detrital zircons.
We thank the reviewer for their thorough comments regarding the data handling and presentation. We have revised each figure and refined the supplemental data material. We address each comment individually below.
As described in Jones et al. (2015), Cenozoic igneous rocks in this region display a clear pattern of more enriched signatures (more “crustal like”) towards the east, as shown by mostly coeval units emplaced in the Frontal Cordillera and the Precordillera. This was ascribed by the authors to the presence of an old basement in the eastern regions (Grenvillian Basement – Cuyania Terrane?) responsible to imprint the enriched signature to the magmas that have transversed it in the eastern region (Precordillera). This had been also recognized earlier by Kay and Abbruzzi (1996) on this same region and by Muñoz et al. (2013) on central Chile (~34°S). A quick look at the data presented in the manuscript that considers the lithologies and the sample location, will reveal that: (1) rocks emplaced in the Frontal Cordillera describe, by themselves, a pattern towards enriched ƐHf signatures from ~28 to 6 Ma, and these data is the one mostly controlling the pattern in blue presented in the ƐHf vs Age diagram in the manuscript, (2) rocks emplaced in the Precordillera also define a pattern towards more enriched ƐHf signatures in time but in a comparatively lower ƐHf trend (more enriched than that of the Frontal Cordillera; note there are also minor juvenile inputs), and these are the samples that mostly control the pattern in red presented in the ƐHf vs Age diagram in the manuscript,
Yes, you make excellent points here. We have observed a similar pattern in longitude vs. zircon ƐHf for a Phanerozoic dataset in the Southern Central Andes (Capaldi et al., 2021- Fig. 10). We determined that inboard arc migration over 800 km produces a shift towards more enriched composition as previously observed by (Chapman et al., 2017; Chapman and Ducea, 2019). The Jones et al., 2015 dataset is spatially limited to -70°S to -69°S: samples were collected mainly in the Frontal Cordillera with one sample (RJ11A5) being truly in the Precordillera across the speculated Chilenia-Cuyania terrane boundary. The variability of average zircon ƐHf in the Frontal Cordillera over the past 300 Myr ranges between +4 and -4 in ƐHf space (Capaldi et al., 2021- Fig. 10). Your point that the zircon ƐHf is purely recording a spatial trend is true to a certain extent, however this mechanism alone cannot fully explain the temporal variations observed in the data. The Jones et al., 2015 samples in the Frontal Cordillera exhibit isotopic pull-downs (samples PC14, RJ11A10, RJ11A11, RJ11A14 between 24-21 Ma; samples RJ11A17, RJ11A15, DI095, MQ33 between 10-6 Ma) and pull-ups (samples SP80, 1026, RF62 between 19-17 Ma; and sample RJ11A7 at 12 Ma). We interpret the temporal variation in the zircon ƐHf to record changes in the magmatic sources driven by crustal thickening associated with underthrusting of fertile crustal material during phases of shortening. We acknowledge your point of a protracted 30 Myr trend in zircon ƐHf signifying enriched magmatic sources that record progressive crustal thickening during Andean Mountain building and spatial trends of the arc across different magmatic sources, we have expanded the text in lines 130-140.

Dear Editor,
In this letter I send you my comments on the revised version of the paper entitled “Inboard advance of arc magmatism regulates mountain building in the Andes” coauthored by Capaldi, T., Horton, B., Mackaman-Lofland, C., Fuentes, F. and Ortiz, G.
In this new version of the manuscript, the authors have taken care of all the minor comments I made in my previous review, yet our disagreement with the interpretation of the Hf isotopic data remains. I see two main issues in this discussion: (i) the scopes and limitations of data from detrital zircons, and (ii) the interpretation of the ƐHf(t) data in terms of the spatial-temporal-compositional analysis. I refer to each of these in the following.
Regarding the detrital zircon data, in my previous review I questioned its use in the model presented by the authors as they have no control over the precise original location of such data in space in the Andean orogen. The authors have replied that it has been shown that this is still a robust tool in tracking the timing and pattern of magmatism. They also add that the data fill in the gaps left by the “petrologist effect” (in bedrock sampling non-altered igneous units) and that it efficiently samples large areas of catchment bedrock sources. I agree with all these statements, yet still the core of my initial critic remains: the detrital data cannot be used for spatial interpretations about the arc, regarding its location and composition at any given time, because there is no control on the original location of such data. I include below a graph of ƐHf(t) vs t diagram (Fig. A) using the data presented by the authors where the detritic data has been separated from the bedrock data in the symbology (small gray dots). As indicated by the authors, the detrital data indeed totally overlaps with the bedrock data and I agree that those zrcs probably come from the Precordillera and the Frontal Cordillera areas. The issue here is that there is no precise control of where those zrcs come from among and within the mentioned areas. The model presented by the authors is fully dependent on a spatial variable, in the location and composition of the arc magmas in time, so detrital data cannot be used for supporting inferences in that respect.
Regarding the interpretations of the ƐHf(t) data, the model presented by the authors predicts a cycle that: (1) starts with arc magmas at a given location with high ƐHf (mantle-like), (2) then the arc magmas show a decreasing ƐHf (more crustal-like) at that same location, (3) then the arc migrates eastwards and magmas show a high ƐHf (mantle-like) starting the cycle again. This model is clearly depicted in Fig. 4 of the manuscript in the previous and the current version of this work. In my previous review I argued against this interpretation based on the actual location of the samples recording the arc location and composition in time (bedrock samples) along with considering previous works in the area. I indicated that Cenozoic igneous rocks in this region show more enriched signatures (more “crustal like”) towards the east, as shown by mostly coeval units emplaced in the Frontal Cordillera and the Precordillera. This was ascribed by Jones et al. (2015), and previously by Kay & Abbruzzi (1996), to the presence of an old basement in the eastern regions (Grenvillian Basement – Cuyania Terrane?) responsible to imprint the enriched signature to the magmas that have transversed it in the eastern region (Precordillera). In their reply, the authors recognize that in this region Andean magmas show progressively more enriched compositions towards the east, but they question my arguments that the ƐHf(t) trend is purely recording a spatial trend indicating that this mechanism alone cannot fully explain the temporal variations observed in the data. Regarding this, there are some misinterpretations on my comments: I do argument that there is a spatial control on the composition of arc magmas, they become generally more enriched towards the east, but this is in addition over imprinted by the general increase in crustal thickness throughout the Andes construction in Cenozoic (from ~22-18 Ma to the present; see Giambiagi & Ramos, 2002; Farías et al., 2010) which adds an increasing crustal signature to progressively younger magmas (lower ƐHf(t) signatures). The ƐHf(t) vs t diagram of Fig. A below shows this very clear for the Frontal Cordillera: igneous rocks emplaced there define a trend towards enriched signatures in time. Moreover, I have included below a map showing the location of all samples discussed in the Capaldi et al. study (detrital and bedrock; Fig. B), where it can be seen that the “trend” for the Frontal Cordillera is constrained by samples very restricted in space (westernmost samples of all those considered in this study; blue dots in Fig. A, B). Regarding rocks emplaced towards the east (in the Precordillera and Precordillera/Frontal Cordillera), as I mentioned in my previous review, they also define a trend towards more enriched ƐHf(t) signatures in time but at a comparatively lower ƐHf values (more enriched than those of the Frontal Cordillera) with minor juvenile inputs.
I must refer to two arguments the authors presented in their reply to discredit the interpretations I discussed above (Jones et al., 2015; Kay & Abbruzzi, 1996). First, they argue that the Jones et al. (2015) dataset is spatially limited to -70°S to -69°S: samples were collected mainly in the Frontal Cordillera with one sample (RJ11A5) being truly in the Precordillera across the speculated Chilenia-Cuyania terrane boundary. I’m not sure where the authors point with this argument: the Jones et al. (2015) data is the only data with spatial location control they have for their model, discrediting this dataset discredits their own spatial-temporal-compositional interpretations. Moreover, the detrital data they present does not add much to the story, given its location and the arguments I presented before regarding such data (see Fig. A, B). Whether limited or not, the Jones et al. (2015) data shows clearly the trends I discussed in the previous paragraph and that are illustrated in Fig. A below. The second argument presented by the authors is that the variability of average zircon ƐHf in the Frontal Cordillera over the past 300 Myr ranges between +4 and -4 in ƐHf space (Capaldi et al., 2021- Fig. 10). I agree, the Fig A below shows this clearly for the Cenozoic: magmas that have transversed the Frontal Cordillera area show a full range of ƐHf(t) values between -4 and +4. The issue here is that, within this range, during Cenozoic there is a temporal evolution to lower signatures (more crustal-like) in younger ages, which is most likely related to the increasing crustal thickness that accompanies the construction of the modern orogen.
In their reply, the authors also present their interpretation of the Jones et al. (2015) data in detail, indicating that samples in the Frontal Cordillera exhibit isotopic pull-downs (samples PC14, RJ11A10, RJ11A11, RJ11A14 between 24-21 Ma; samples RJ11A17, RJ11A15, DI095, MQ33 between 10-6 Ma) and pull-ups (samples SP80, 1026, RF62 between 19-17 Ma; and sample RJ11A7 at 12 Ma). The problem here is what they are considering as located in the Frontal Cordillera or elsewhere. Setting aside “names”, Figs. A and B below show that within the full age range considered the spatially restricted group of westernmost samples (in blue in the figures) is comparatively more depleted (mantle-like) than coeval magmas emplaced in eastern regions except for local juvenile inputs (2 samples at ~24 and 12 Ma).
The authors have added to the new version of the manuscript a paragraph that describes general aspects of the arc magmas composition in the studied region. They indicate there that: “Coupled zircon geochemical and age data exhibit a progressive decrease in zircon εHf values over the last 30 Myr (Fig. 3B). When considered alongside with bedrock sample locations (Fig. 2A), a spatial relationship emerges: relatively asthenospheric (juvenile) compositions are preferentially located near the trench, in contrast while more lithospheric (evolved) contributions are concentrated toward the craton (Fig. 3B). Superimposed on this 30 Myr trend are higher-frequency phases (5-8 Myr) in which the relatively depleted positive εHf values represent background arc magmatism generated by juvenile mantle sources, which were perturbed during isotopic pull-downs phases reflecting greater contribution of evolved crustal sources (Fig. 3B). A 1 to 2 Myr temporal overlap in both depleted and enriched values are observed at the onset of the isotopic pull-down indicating magma mixing processes during changes in magmatic source (Hawkesworth and Kemp, 2006)”. The processes described here, and the model depicted in Fig. 4 of the manuscript, are not supported by the data. For example, there is not a single sample from the spatially restricted westernmost group of the Fontal Cordillera that describes an “isotopic pull down” from the general trend they described through Cenozoic (blue spots in Fig A); the comparatively lower ƐHf signatures are described exclusively by samples located to the east. Moreover, the model presented by the authors predicts a zig-zag ƐHf trend marked by high and low values developing sequentially in time towards the east: this is by no means described by data with spatial control (Fig A, B).
In summary, I consider that the model presented by the authors is attractive and can explain several geological observations. However, in my opinion the magmatic evolution this model entails, in terms of the sequential variation in arc location and its composition, is not supported by the data.
Best regards.

predicts a cycle that: (1) starts with arc magmas at a given location with high ƐHf (mantle-like), (2) then the arc magmas show a decreasing ƐHf (more crustal-like) at that same location, (3) then the arc migrates eastwards and magmas show a high ƐHf (mantle-like) starting the cycle again. This model is clearly depicted in Fig. 4 of the manuscript in the previous and the current version of this work. In my previous review I argued against this interpretation based on the actual location of the samples recording the arc location and composition in time (bedrock samples) along with considering previous works in the area.
I must refer to two arguments the authors presented in their reply to discredit the interpretations I discussed above (Jones et al., 2015; Kay & Abbruzzi, 1996). First, they argue that the Jones et al. (2015) dataset is spatially limited to -70°S to -69°S: samples were collected mainly in the Frontal Cordillera with one sample (RJ11A5) being truly in the Precordillera across the speculated Chilenia-Cuyania terrane boundary. I’m not sure where the authors point with this argument: the Jones et al. (2015) data is the only data with spatial location control they have for their model, discrediting this dataset discredits their own spatial-temporal compositional interpretations. Moreover, the detrital data they present does not add much to the story, given its location and the arguments I presented before regarding such data (see Fig. A, B). Whether limited or not, the Jones et al. (2015) data shows clearly the trends I discussed in the previous paragraph and that are illustrated in Fig. A below. The second argument presented by the authors is that the variability of average zircon ƐHf in the Frontal Cordillera over the past 300 Myr ranges between +4 and -4 in ƐHf space (Capaldi et al., 2021- Fig. 10). I agree, the Fig A below
2
shows this clearly for the Cenozoic: magmas that have transversed the Frontal Cordillera area show a full range of ƐHf(t) values between -4 and +4. The issue here is that, within this range, during Cenozoic there is a temporal evolution to lower signatures (more crustal-like) in younger ages, which is most likely related to the increasing crustal thickness that accompanies the construction of the modern orogen.
In their reply, the authors also present their interpretation of the Jones et al. (2015) data in detail, indicating that samples in the Frontal Cordillera exhibit isotopic pull-downs (samples PC14, RJ11A10, RJ11A11, RJ11A14 between 24-21 Ma; samples RJ11A17, J11A15, DI095, MQ33 between 10-6 Ma) and pull-ups (samples SP80, 1026, RF62 between 19-17 Ma; and sample RJ11A7 at 12 Ma). The problem here is what they are considering as located in the Frontal Cordillera or elsewhere. Setting aside “names”, Figs. A and B below show that within the full age range considered the spatially restricted group of westernmost samples (in blue in the figures) is comparatively more depleted (mantle-like) than coeval magmas emplaced in eastern regions except for local juvenile inputs (2 samples at ~24 and 12 Ma).
The authors have added to the new version of the manuscript a paragraph that describes general aspects of the arc magmas composition in the studied region. They indicate there that: “Coupled zircon geochemical and age data exhibit a progressive decrease in zircon εHf values over the last 30 Myr (Fig. 3B). When considered alongside with bedrock sample locations (Fig. 2A), a spatial relationship emerges: relatively asthenospheric (juvenile) compositions are preferentially located near the trench, in contrast while more lithospheric (evolved) contributions are concentrated toward the craton (Fig. 3B). Superimposed on this 30 Myr trend are higher-frequency phases (5-8 Myr) in which the relatively depleted positive εHf values represent background arc magmatism generated by juvenile mantle sources, which were perturbed during isotopic pull-downs phases reflecting greater contribution of evolved crustal sources (Fig. 3B). A 1 to 2 Myr temporal overlap in both depleted and enriched values are observed at the onset of the isotopic pull-down indicating magma mixing processes during changes in magmatic source (Hawkesworth and Kemp, 2006)”. The processes described here, and the model depicted in Fig. 4 of the manuscript, are not supported by the data. For example, there is not a single sample from the spatially restricted westernmost group of the Fontal Cordillera that describes an “isotopic pull down” from the general trend they described through Cenozoic (blue spots in Fig A); the comparatively lower ƐHf signatures are described exclusively by samples located to the east. Moreover, the model presented by the authors predicts a zigzag ƐHf trend marked by high and low values developing sequentially in time towards the east: this is by no means described by data with spatial control (Fig A, B).
In summary, I consider that the model presented by the authors is attractive and can explain several geological observations. However, in my opinion the magmatic
3
evolution this model entails, in terms of the sequential variation in arc location and its composition, is not supported by the data.

Response to Reviewer 2
We appreciate Reviewer 2’s evaluation of our manuscript. Their detailed comments have helped us clarify key points in our revised manuscript in support of our tectonic reconstruction of the southern central Andes, with broader implications for Cordilleran systems.
Reviewer 2 raises two main concerns regarding our interpretation of the isotopic data: (1) the spatial limitations of detrital zircon datasets, and (2) the validity of our multi-phase model for magmatic source evolution. They argue that detrital data, while useful for tracking temporal trends, cannot reliably constrain spatial relationships due to uncertain provenance. Additionally, they propose a spatially anchored model in which magmatic compositions become progressively more enriched toward the east, overprinted by a gradual increase in crustal thickness through time, which results in a smooth, monotonic decline in ƐHf values. In contrast, our model emphasizes episodic shifts in magmatic source linked to deformation-driven processes such as underthrusting and arc widening. Below, we carefully consider the alternative conceptual model presented by Reviewer 2, point out several limitations in their model, and show how our interpretation (utilizing results from both bedrock and detrital materials) provides a more compelling case that is supported by extensive isotopic, geochronologic, and structural/stratigraphic data.
1. Spatial Control and the Role of Detrital Zircon Geochemistry:
While we acknowledge that detrital datasets can be spatially diffuse and subject to mixing, this limitation does not preclude their utility—particularly when interpreted in tandem with spatially constrained in-situ bedrock data. In fact, the close correspondence between detrital zircon compositions and those of Frontal Cordillera and Precordillera igneous centers reinforces their provenance and validates their use in tracking temporal shifts in magmatic geochemistry.
Rather than dismissing detrital data outright, we argue that its strength lies in capturing basin-wide signals of magmatic evolution, especially in regions where bedrock exposures are discontinuous, structurally complex, or biased by sampling limitations. When integrated with latitudinally and longitudinally resolved bedrock datasets, detrital zircon geochemistry provides a robust framework for reconstructing temporal and geochemical trends across the arc system. This integrated approach enables us to detect episodic shifts in magmatic source and arc position that would be obscured by relying solely on bedrock samples.
2. Temporal Variability in Magmatic Sources:
Reviewer 2 proposes an alternative conceptual model that makes two key predictions. First, a prolonged, linear decrease in zircon ƐHf values in the Frontal Cordillera—such that successive magmatic phases yield progressively lower values through time. Second, in contrast, Precordillera magmatism is predicted to follow a parallel trend, offset towards more negative values, reflecting its recycled, evolved crustal signature.
However, this linear trend is not supported by the data. Instead, both Frontal Cordillera and Precordillera datasets exhibit a step-wise pattern: juvenile (positive) εHf values shift toward more enriched (negative) compositions, then rebound to more juvenile values. To reinforce this interpretation, we have incorporated whole-rock ƐNd data from the Frontal Cordillera, Precordillera, and Sierras Pampeanas, complied by Kay et al., (1999) and drawn from her earlier studies (Kay et al., 1991; Kay and Gordillo, 1994; Kay and Abbruzzi, 1996).
Given the well-established coherence between Hf-Lu and Nd-Sm isotopic systems (e.g., Patchett et al., 1981; Vervoort et al., 2000; Chapman et al., 2017), these εNd data provide an independent and spatially constrained line of evidence for variability in magmatic geochemistry. The combined zircon εHf and whole-rock εNd datasets clearly demonstrate step-wise isotopic pull-downs and subsequent pull-ups in the magmatic systems. These short-timescale fluctuations are superimposed on the broader 30 Myr trend toward more enriched signatures, supporting our interpretation of episodic crustal thickening and source evolution during discrete shortening phases (see Fig. A).
3. Misunderstanding of the Multi-Phase Model
We respectfully disagree with Reviewer 2’s interpretation of our multi-phase model. Reviewer 2 summarizes our model as predicting a cycle that “ (1) starts with arc magmas at a given location with high ƐHf (mantle-like), (2) then the arc magmas show a decreasing ƐHf (more crustal-like) at that same location.” This characterization misrepresents the spatial dynamic central to our model.
Our model emphasizes the evolving relationship between the arc front and the deformation front, highlighting the lag between initial magmatic migration inboard and the onset of deformation. In this framework, slab-derived fluids weaken the foreland lithosphere, inducing deformation that generates upper crustal loading and flexural subsidence. This is coeval with middle to lower crustal underthrusting, which triggers a high-flux magmatic event (HFE) characterized by enriched isotopic signatures.

Detrital zircon εHf (yellow circles) match the bedrock isotopic trends.

The location of this data is central to the interpretations and differences between a reviewer and the authors. Given the implications of the proposed model to other convergent margins, linking Figure 1 to Figure 3 is essential for interpreting spatial trends. I had assumed the age of the circles and diamonds from Figure 3 (x-axis) correspond with the location of the data (Main Cordillera, Frontal, Pre, Sierras Pampeanas) as shown by the grey bars. However, the figure provided by Reviewer 2 clearly shows that some of the young (e.g., <10 Ma) zircons are from the Frontal Cordillera, not the regions farther east. You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Debate continues over the mechanisms that govern the tempo and style of arc magmatism and retroarc deformation along ocean-continent plate boundaries. Here we integrate detrital and bedrock geo/thermochronological and geochemical records of Cenozoic arc magmatism with results on the spatiotemporal evolution of retroarc shortening and flexural subsidence to explore the interactions and feedbacks among subduction, magmatism, and crustal deformation in the southern Central Andes. A synthesis of igneous compositions, magmatic activity, thrust belt shortening, and sediment accumulation reveals recurring phases of increased arc magmatism, retroarc underthrusting, and foreland basin development over short (<10 Myr) timescales. Episodic advance of deformation was focused within discrete Andean tectonic provinces (of contrasting pre-Andean inheritance) that were sequentially activated toward the foreland along newly formed middle/upper-crustal décollements. Inboard migration of arc magmatism consistently preceded deformation advance, suggesting that fluid-assisted weakening above the subducting slab facilitated enhanced shortening and orogenic growth toward the cratonic interior.

---

## Introduction

Interactions between arc magmatism and retroarc deformation shape topography, climate, and basin evolution in Andean-type orogenic systems along ocean-continent convergent margins. These relationships may represent responses to external drivers and/or internally coordinated processes that strongly influence crustal shortening, igneous activity, and basin subsidence. The underlying mechanisms responsible for time-space variations in tectonic and magmatic processes remain poorly understood. Most models linking the rates and magnitudes of arc magmatism and retroarc deformation have centered on cyclical behavior in orogens characterized by large-scale (>200–300 km) horizontal shortening, extreme crustal thickening (>60–70 km Moho depth), and episodic removal of thickened lower crust/lithosphere through foundering or delamination1,2,3,4. Such cycles occur over long timescales (>20–50 Myr) and preferentially affect only the largest and thickest orogenic systems. However, potential internal cycles of shorter duration (<10 Myr) may also operate during mountain building, particularly in regions of lower-magnitude (<50–150 km) shortening. Here we hypothesize that short-term orogenic phases linked to shifts in thermal and rheological conditions help regulate dynamic interactions among subduction, arc magmatism, and retroarc deformation.

Evaluating Andean-type orogenesis requires consideration of diverse mechanisms that affect spatial-temporal patterns in arc magmatism and retroarc shortening. Arc migration toward the continental interior has been associated with heightened magmatic activity along subduction margins5. Such landward migration expands slab dewatering within the mantle wedge, enhancing fluid flux and hydration of the overriding foreland lithosphere6, which may further induce crustal weakening and strain localization7.

A range of internal and external mechanisms within the upper and lower plates may account for inboard advance of arc magmatism8. Internally, within the overriding plate, arc advance may be a product of retroarc shortening9 and/or forearc subduction erosion 10,11. In addition, arc advance may be driven by external forces that affect the subducting plate, including accelerated plate convergence12 or low-angle (flat slab) subduction13,14,15,16. Although slab shallowing is commonly attributed to subduction of buoyant (i.e., younger or thicker) oceanic lithosphere, several studies indicate a poor correlation among oceanic slab age, crustal thickness, seafloor asperities, and slab dip17,18. Alternatively, slab shallowing may be driven by the position of thick continental lithospheric roots that promote hydrodynamic suction (or negative pressure) associated with corner flow in the mantle wedge between the subducting and overriding plates 19,20. Because the aforementioned interactions vary over a range of spatial and temporal scales, it is important to identify the processes responsible for arc migration and assess their impact on short-term (<10 Myr) changes in magmatism and retroarc orogenesis within Cordilleran systems.

In this study, we compare the spatial, temporal, and compositional variations of arc magmatism in the southern Central Andes with geo/thermochronological, geochemical, and stratigraphic datasets to better understand the geodynamic links among subduction, magmatism, and Andean orogenesis. The modern Pampean segment (27–33° S) of the Nazca-South American plate boundary (Fig. 1) is characterized by flat slab subduction, a ~500 km long gap in active volcanism, and foreland basement uplifts of the Sierras Pampeanas located >700 km inboard of the trench (Fig. 1A)15, 21, 22, 23, 24. Our analysis focuses on the past 30 Myr of mountain building in western Argentina, a region characterized by persistently arid climatic conditions25,26, which enables the isolation of tectonic signals associated with orogenic wedge behavior. Synthesizing records of Andean arc magmatism and retroarc deformation provides the opportunity to explore the feedbacks between subducting and overriding plates to identify potentially cyclical mechanisms that regulate mountain building along convergent plate boundaries.

---

## Results

Magmatic Arc Activity and Composition

To assess time-space patterns of arc magmatism and retroarc crustal shortening, we compile crystallization ages of Cenozoic igneous rocks along an arc-normal east-west profile (Fig. 2A). These regional patterns in arc magmatism (Fig. 2A) are compared with arc tempo and magmatic compositional data registered in whole-rock and zircon minerals (Fig. 3B and 3C). Geochronological results paired with εHf and εNd isotopic compositions provide valuable temporal recorders of continental arc evolution that are sensitive to upper-crustal composition and crystallization conditions. Positive εHf and εNd values reflect juvenile crustal material originating from melts of depleted (juvenile) mantle origin, whereas negative isotopic values signify enriched melts derived from older, recycled (evolved) crustal material27, 28, 29.

The geochemical match between detrital zircon εHf values and those of spatially resolved igneous bedrock (Fig. 3A) strengthens confidence in their provenance and demonstrates their value as a complementary tool for tracking magmatic evolution through time. Detrital zircon age distributions for continental magmatic arcs and their associated basins are robust temporal indicators of arc activity, suitable for tracking rates of zircon-bearing arc-magma production and identifying punctuated high-volume magmatic events in the form of flare-ups or high-flux events (HFEs)30,31,32.

Oligocene arc magmatism (33–25 Ma) was focused over a narrow (~100 km wide) zone within the Main Cordillera (Fig. 2A). Compositionally, these magmas exhibit positive εHf and εNd values, indicative of depleted mantle wedge sources (Fig. 3B). By 25 Ma, the arc advanced eastward, forming a broader (~200 km wide) zone that spanned the Main and Frontal Cordilleras (Fig. 2A). During the late Oligocene to early Miocene (25–19 Ma) zircon εHf trends delineate an isotopic pull-down toward enriched magma sources contemporaneous with increased arc activity recorded by greater proportions of detrital zircon ages (Fig. 3B and 3C). ### Reviewer 2

Dear Editor,
In this letter I send you my comments on the revised version of the paper entitled “Inboard advance of arc magmatism regulates mountain building in the Andes” coauthored by Capaldi, T., Horton, B., Mackaman-Lofland, C., Fuentes, F. and Ortiz, G.
In this new version of the manuscript, the authors have taken care of all the minor comments I made in my previous review, yet our disagreement with the interpretation of the Hf isotopic data remains. I see two main issues in this discussion: (i) the scopes and limitations of data from detrital zircons, and (ii) the interpretation of the ƐHf(t) data in terms of the spatial-temporal-compositional analysis. I refer to each of these in the following.
Regarding the detrital zircon data, in my previous review I questioned its use in the model presented by the authors as they have no control over the precise original location of such data in space in the Andean orogen. The authors have replied that it has been shown that this is still a robust tool in tracking the timing and pattern of magmatism. They also add that the data fill in the gaps left by the “petrologist effect” (in bedrock sampling non-altered igneous units) and that it efficiently samples large areas of catchment bedrock sources. I agree with all these statements, yet still the core of my initial critic remains: the detrital data cannot be used for spatial interpretations about the arc, regarding its location and composition at any given time, because there is no control on the original location of such data. I include below a graph of ƐHf(t) vs t diagram (Fig. A) using the data presented by the authors where the detritic data has been separated from the bedrock data in the symbology (small gray dots). As indicated by the authors, the detrital data indeed totally overlaps with the bedrock data and I agree that those zrcs probably come from the Precordillera and the Frontal Cordillera areas. The issue here is that there is no precise control of where those zrcs come from among and within the mentioned areas. The model presented by the authors is fully dependent on a spatial variable, in the location and composition of the arc magmas in time, so detrital data cannot be used for supporting inferences in that respect.
Regarding the interpretations of the ƐHf(t) data, the model presented by the authors predicts a cycle that: (1) starts with arc magmas at a given location with high ƐHf (mantle-like), (2) then the arc magmas show a decreasing ƐHf (more crustal-like) at that same location, (3) then the arc migrates eastwards and magmas show a high ƐHf (mantle-like) starting the cycle again. This model is clearly depicted in Fig. 4 of the manuscript in the previous and the current version of this work. In my previous review I argued against this interpretation based on the actual location of the samples recording the arc location and composition in time (bedrock samples) along with considering previous works in the area. I indicated that Cenozoic igneous rocks in this region show more enriched signatures (more “crustal like”) towards the east, as shown by mostly coeval units emplaced in the Frontal Cordillera and the Precordillera. This was ascribed by Jones et al. (2015), and previously by Kay & Abbruzzi (1996), to the presence of an old basement in the eastern regions (Grenvillian Basement – Cuyania Terrane?) responsible to imprint the enriched signature to the magmas that have transversed it in the eastern region (Precordillera). In their reply, the authors recognize that in this region Andean magmas show progressively more enriched compositions towards the east, but they question my arguments that the ƐHf(t) trend is purely recording a spatial trend indicating that this mechanism alone cannot fully explain the temporal variations observed in the data. Regarding this, there are some misinterpretations on my comments: I do argument that there is a spatial control on the composition of arc magmas, they become generally more enriched towards the east, but this is in addition over imprinted by the general increase in crustal thickness throughout the Andes construction in Cenozoic (from ~22-18 Ma to the present; see Giambiagi & Ramos, 2002; Farías et al., 2010) which adds an increasing crustal signature to progressively younger magmas (lower ƐHf(t) signatures). The ƐHf(t) vs t diagram of Fig. A below shows this very clear for the Frontal Cordillera: igneous rocks emplaced there define a trend towards enriched signatures in time. Moreover, I have included below a map showing the location of all samples discussed in the Capaldi et al. study (detrital and bedrock; Fig. B), where it can be seen that the “trend” for the Frontal Cordillera is constrained by samples very restricted in space (westernmost samples of all those considered in this study; blue dots in Fig. A, B). Regarding rocks emplaced towards the east (in the Precordillera and Precordillera/Frontal Cordillera), as I mentioned in my previous review, they also define a trend towards more enriched ƐHf(t) signatures in time but at a comparatively lower ƐHf values (more enriched than those of the Frontal Cordillera) with minor juvenile inputs.
I must refer to two arguments the authors presented in their reply to discredit the interpretations I discussed above (Jones et al., 2015; Kay & Abbruzzi, 1996). First, they argue that the Jones et al. (2015) dataset is spatially limited to -70°S to -69°S: samples were collected mainly in the Frontal Cordillera with one sample (RJ11A5) being truly in the Precordillera across the speculated Chilenia-Cuyania terrane boundary. I’m not sure where the authors point with this argument: the Jones et al. (2015) data is the only data with spatial location control they have for their model, discrediting this dataset discredits their own spatial-temporal-compositional interpretations. Moreover, the detrital data they present does not add much to the story, given its location and the arguments I presented before regarding such data (see Fig. A, B). Whether limited or not, the Jones et al. (2015) data shows clearly the trends I discussed in the previous paragraph and that are illustrated in Fig. A below. The second argument presented by the authors is that the variability of average zircon ƐHf in the Frontal Cordillera over the past 300 Myr ranges between +4 and -4 in ƐHf space (Capaldi et al., 2021- Fig. 10). I agree, the Fig A below shows this clearly for the Cenozoic: magmas that have transversed the Frontal Cordillera area show a full range of ƐHf(t) values between -4 and +4. The issue here is that, within this range, during Cenozoic there is a temporal evolution to lower signatures (more crustal-like) in younger ages, which is most likely related to the increasing crustal thickness that accompanies the construction of the modern orogen.
In their reply, the authors also present their interpretation of the Jones et al. (2015) data in detail, indicating that samples in the Frontal Cordillera exhibit isotopic pull-downs (samples PC14, RJ11A10, RJ11A11, RJ11A14 between 24-21 Ma; samples RJ11A17, RJ11A15, DI095, MQ33 between 10-6 Ma) and pull-ups (samples SP80, 1026, RF62 between 19-17 Ma; and sample RJ11A7 at 12 Ma). The problem here is what they are considering as located in the Frontal Cordillera or elsewhere. Setting aside “names”, Figs. A and B below show that within the full age range considered the spatially restricted group of westernmost samples (in blue in the figures) is comparatively more depleted (mantle-like) than coeval magmas emplaced in eastern regions except for local juvenile inputs (2 samples at ~24 and 12 Ma).
The authors have added to the new version of the manuscript a paragraph that describes general aspects of the arc magmas composition in the studied region. They indicate there that: “Coupled zircon geochemical and age data exhibit a progressive decrease in zircon εHf values over the last 30 Myr (Fig. 3B). When considered alongside with bedrock sample locations (Fig. 2A), a spatial relationship emerges: relatively asthenospheric (juvenile) compositions are preferentially located near the trench, in contrast while more lithospheric (evolved) contributions are concentrated toward the craton (Fig. 3B). Superimposed on this 30 Myr trend are higher-frequency phases (5-8 Myr) in which the relatively depleted positive εHf values represent background arc magmatism generated by juvenile mantle sources, which were perturbed during isotopic pull-downs phases reflecting greater contribution of evolved crustal sources (Fig. 3B). A 1 to 2 Myr temporal overlap in both depleted and enriched values are observed at the onset of the isotopic pull-down indicating magma mixing processes during changes in magmatic source (Hawkesworth and Kemp, 2006)”. The processes described here, and the model depicted in Fig. 4 of the manuscript, are not supported by the data. For example, there is not a single sample from the spatially restricted westernmost group of the Fontal Cordillera that describes an “isotopic pull down” from the general trend they described through Cenozoic (blue spots in Fig A); the comparatively lower ƐHf signatures are described exclusively by samples located to the east. Moreover, the model presented by the authors predicts a zig-zag ƐHf trend marked by high and low values developing sequentially in time towards the east: this is by no means described by data with spatial control (Fig A, B).
In summary, I consider that the model presented by the authors is attractive and can explain several geological observations. However, in my opinion the magmatic evolution this model entails, in terms of the sequential variation in arc location and its composition, is not supported by the data.
Best regards.
